series.title: Camera Architecture
series.description: 12-part series from photons to final image: what 48 MP actually means, optics, sensor, ISP, compute, algorithms and software tuning.

episodes.title: What Does 48 Megapixels Actually Mean?
episodes.excerpt: First one. 48 MP = ~48 million pixels (e.g. 8000×6000). Pixel = [R,G,B]. More pixels ≠ automatically more detail.

body.text: When a smartphone says 48 MP camera, what exactly are those 48 million? It doesn't mean 48 million colors, 48x zoom, or automatically better quality.
It means the sensor can produce roughly 48,000,000 pixels. Example: 8000 x 6000 = 48,000,000, so 48,000,000 / 1,000,000 = 48 MP. Megapixels = (Width x Height) / 1,000,000.
But what is a pixel?

A digital image is a 2D matrix I(x, y). For color, a pixel eventually holds Pixel = [R, G, B]. So a 48 MP RGB image holds about 48,000,000 x 3 = 144 million channel values before other representations and processing.
Does more MP mean better quality?

Not necessarily. Quality depends on sensor size, pixel pitch, lens quality, noise, dynamic range, bit depth, ISP and computational photography. More pixels does not automatically mean more detail if the lens cannot resolve it or noise dominates.
Megapixels ≠ Megabytes

Megapixels count spatial samples. Storage depends on bits per pixel and encoding. Example: 24 MP RGB at 8 bits per channel is about 24,000,000 x 3 bytes ≈ 72 MB uncompressed — JPEG reduces this dramatically.
If a sensor produces tens of millions of measurements, how does a phone process it in real time? Next: what happens inside a single pixel — photons → electrons → signals → digital values.

episodes.title: Why Two Phones With Similar Cameras Take Different Photos
episodes.excerpt: Final part. The sensor is only one part: optics, ISP, compute, algorithms and tuning define the photo. 48 MP isn't the photograph.

body.text: We started this series asking: what does 48 MP actually mean? 12 parts later, one final question: if two phones use similar sensors, why do their photos look completely different?
The answer is simple: the sensor is only one part of the camera system.
What actually defines a camera?

items: Optics — lens sharpness, distortion, light transmission
Sensor — pixel pitch, dynamic range, bit depth, size: 48 MP A ≠ 48 MP B
ISP — demosaicing, noise reduction, white balance, tone mapping: RAW ≠ final photo
Silicon & compute — CPU + GPU + NPU + ISP sharing real-time workloads
Algorithms — HDR, Night Mode, portrait segmentation, super-resolution
Software tuning — color profiles, contrast, skin-tone choices

body.text: Camera Performance = f(Optics, Sensor, ISP, Compute, Memory, Algorithms, Software)
Physics provides photons → sensor measures → electronics digitizes → ISP processes → compute accelerates → memory moves data → algorithms reconstruct → codecs compress → software displays.
Does 200 MP beat 48 MP? No. More megapixels give more samples, but quality depends on the entire pipeline. 48 MP isn't the photograph, it's just one number in a larger system.

series.title: Understanding Grafana Metrics
series.description: 15-part series moving from single metrics to metric families, app behavior, infrastructure and root-cause troubleshooting. Goal: stop memorizing metric names, start understanding the story behind the numbers.

episodes.title: Why Does This Number Change?
episodes.excerpt: A metric is a live reflection of an event in your app. Trace a real request: Nginx → Django → DB → Prometheus → Grafana.

body.text: If you've worked with Grafana, you've seen dashboards filled with charts: CPU usage, request latency, DB queries, HTTP requests. But have you ever stopped to ask: what actually makes this value change?
A metric isn't just a random number on a panel. It's a live reflection of an event inside your application.
Trace a real user request
So when django_db_execute_total moves, it's not generic activity. It means a specific database execution just happened.
The debugging lesson
When latency spikes, that single number won't tell you the root cause. Debugging isn't reading numbers, it's connecting the dots:
HTTP Latency → Django View → DB Query Duration → DB Connections → CPU Usage
The real power of observability comes from understanding how these metrics relate to each other.

episodes.title: Counter, Gauge, Histogram & Summary
episodes.excerpt: Not all metrics behave the same. Counter only goes up, Gauge moves up and down, Histogram buckets latency, Summary pre-computes quantiles.

body.text: Before you start reading Grafana charts, there's a core rule: not all metrics behave the same way. A value that only increases (like total errors) must be interpreted differently from a value that goes up and down (like CPU usage).
1. Counter — How many have happened total?

items: Only goes UP (or resets to 0 on restart)
Examples: total requests, total errors, django_db_execute_total

body.text: Tip: look at the rate of change, not just the raw total.
2. Gauge — What is the value right now?

items: Examples: CPU 40% → 75% → 52%, memory, active DB connections, queue size

body.text: 3. Histogram — How are observations distributed?
Essential for latency. Don't rely on averages. Groups data into buckets (e.g. how many requests took ≤0.1s, ≤0.5s, ≤2s). Exposes _bucket, _count and _sum.
4. Summary — What are the calculated quantiles?
Also for latency, but calculates percentiles client-side. Example: p50 = 0.2s, p90 = 0.7s, p99 = 2.4s. Directly answers: how slow are my worst-case requests?
Cheat sheet

django_db_execute_total and django_db_query_duration_seconds_bucket are both database metrics, but need different functions (rate() vs histogram_quantile()) to chart correctly. Know your metric type before you build your panel.
